hero.headline: Whether you know your gender or not, it's time to understand it.

definition.sense: to cause or give rise to a feeling, situation or condition.

hero.subheadline: Give time and context to your feelings. Keep a diary and track your gender with either proposed or custom-made scales. After a while, check out the statistics and learn something new about your gender!

promises.heading: Free, for good.
promises.body: No price, no plan, no ads. The app is available at GPLv3 license. It's also open source, which means you'll never see an ad or a paid subscription here.

promises.heading: Nothing to sell.
promises.body: The app has no backend or a concept of an account. Your journal is stored solely on your device, encrypted. You don't have to trust anyone not to sell your most intimate data - I cannot sell what I do not have.

promises.heading: All of it, in one place.
promises.body: Journal, stats, HRT, surgeries, tryouts, eras, voice practice and a printable summary for your clinician.

promises.heading: By trans people, for trans people.
promises.body: The app is made by one trans person from Warsaw, Poland. There is no company or corporation behind it.

overview: engender is where you keep your transition: how you feel from day to day, what HRT you take, what you are trying out (such as a name or pronouns), what is coming up (surgeries, appointments) and what has already happened (milestones, eras). It is a journal first. Around it are several modules focused on various aspects of a gender transition.

Nothing in it decides anything about you. You name your own scales and pick what to track, and the app will never judge you for anything. engender knows, that every transition is different - that's why in settings you can set which features/modules are of interest for you and which can be hidden.
It is free software: there is no price, no plan and nothing to upsell, and the licence keeps it that way.
sectionPrivacy: What it protects from, and what it doesn't
privacyHandoff: Your journal stays on your device. There is no engender account, no server, and no copy of your entries anywhere but where you put them. I cannot read your journal, but I also cannot recover it.

On your device it is encrypted, and you choose what opens it: a passphrase, a PIN, your fingerprint or face, or the device's own lock. On Android the app does not even ask for internet permission. In a browser, the web host sees the app being loaded and checking for updates, and nothing of what you write.
If you would rather not rely on my server at all, you can host the app yourself: every release publishes it as a bundle you can serve from your own server.

tour.caption: The greeting, what is coming up, and the parts of the app you pinned there. The mood faces log an entry for right now in one action, so on a day when you cannot face writing, you can still log something.
Mood, your scales, tags, a note, photos. Only the mood is required, so a day where all you managed was a mood is still a day you logged.
Coloured by mood, or by any scale you choose.
Gender can shift through a day, so a day holds as many entries as it needs and stamps each one with its time. The day's own colour is their average.
Search your notes and your tags as you type.
Every scale gets its own chart and its own average over however many days you pick.
Dated days that matter, in order. The ones ahead count down. The ones behind come back each year as a reminder of good times.
Export packs everything into one Archive, encrypted with a password you choose.
The same passage recorded today and a month ago, side by side. Pitch, resonance and speaking rate describe each take.

paragraphs.rest: Export packs your journal into one file, encrypted with a password you choose Import puts it back, either merged into what is here or replacing it.
On Android, an encrypted Archive saved weekly or monthly to a folder you pick, on the phone or with a cloud provider. The app shows when the last one worked and when one failed.
Import a Daylio CSV or a Daylio backup. It shows you the counts and how the moods will map before it writes anything.
CSV or JSON. It is not encrypted, so use at your own discretion!
If your last backup is more than 30 days old, the app will remind you to make a backup. Can be turned off.
It works offline and never even asks for internet permission, so the app has no way to send your journal anywhere.
Once or repeating, as notifications on your phone. A medication reminder opens that drug's dose log, with Taken and Skip on the notification itself.
One prompt a day, at a time you choose, skipped on days you have already written something.
Add it to your home screen and open it without a browser in the way.
Once it is installed it does not need the network to open.

paragraphs: Choose how to unlock the journal in Privacy and data. The journal can stay fully unlocked, but you can also lock it with PIN, password or a fingerprint. You can also use a disguise function that changes your lock screen, the app icon and it's name in the app drawer to neutral ones.

paragraphs.rest: Use a passphrase, a PIN with a device key, supported biometrics or a device-bound key.

The browser tab says Notes instead of engender. On Android, the app takes a neutral name and icon, and the lock screen, widgets and notifications stop naming it. Once the journal is unlocked, nothing inside changes.
The journal can lock as soon as you switch away, after one or five minutes away, or only when the app restarts.
: trans, nonbinary, genderfluid, bisexual, lesbian, pansexual, rainbow, agender, gay men, genderqueer, intersex, asexual, demiboy, demigirl, trigender and the Polish flag.
English and Polish

acquisitionIntro: engender runs in a browser. It opens straight away, with nothing to install and no account to make.
acquisitionAndroid: The Android app is the same journal as an app. These are the four places to get it, and each becomes a link as it goes live. Google Play is last for a reason.

channels.name: Aurora
channels.note: The same build as Google Play, without your Google account attached to the download.

channels.name: F-Droid
channels.note: Builds the app from source itself, so you are not trusting a file that came from me.

channels.name: Obtainium
channels.note: Follows this project's releases on GitHub and keeps itself up to date.

channels.name: Google Play
channels.note: Works, and tells Google you have a trans app on your phone. Nothing in engender changes that.

support: I'm Alicja Barankiewicz, a data engineer in Warsaw. I also run nazwozbior.pl, which searches every name in the Polish PESEL registry for anyone looking for the one that fits.

support.rest: engender is free software under the GPLv3. The source is public.

support: The licence means you can run it, change it and pass it on, and it cannot be taken back. If I stop, someone else is free to pick the code up, and your Archives are a documented format rather than something only this app can open.

privacyPage.title: Privacy policy
privacyPage.intro: Last updated: 2026-11-11 engender is a journal for tracking a gender transition, made and published by Alicja Barankiewicz in Warsaw, Poland. This policy covers the Android app, the web app, the website and guide, and support messages.
privacyPage.guideLink: Read the Privacy chapter in the Guide.

sections.heading: Contact
paragraphs: Email: engender-app@pm.me
Bugs and general questions: https://github.com/engender-app/engender/issues
Security problems: https://github.com/engender-app/engender/blob/main/SECURITY.md
You never need to send journal content, a backup file or a key to get help.

sections.heading: Your journal
paragraphs: There is no engender account and no server holding your journal. Your journal stays on your device, and none of it is sent to the developer or to anyone else. Its database and media are encrypted at rest.

Two things sit outside that encryption. What the app needs before you unlock it is stored unencrypted: theme, palette, language, disguise, lock timing and the details of how the journal unlocks. On Android, a photo you take passes through an unencrypted temporary file in the app's cache before engender imports and encrypts it.

sections.heading: Lost keys and passwords
paragraphs: The developer cannot recover a forgotten passphrase, PIN or backup password, or a lost device key or recovery key.

sections.heading: Android app
paragraphs: The Android app does not request the INTERNET permission. It opens no network connections and sends nothing to any server. It also opts out of Android's cloud backup and device-to-device transfer. Wherever you download the app from (GitHub, Google Play or F-Droid) handles that download under its own terms.

Android itself does a few things the app can only partly control. The app opts out of WebView diagnostic uploads to Google, but Google Safe Browsing stays at WebView's enabled default, and its checks can use Google Play services' network access. The app asks your keyboard not to learn what you type, and the keyboard can ignore that. Your keyboard and browser can make their own network requests independently of engender.
The app has these permissions:
POST_NOTIFICATIONS, SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM and RECEIVE_BOOT_COMPLETED for reminders at the time you set, including after a restart.
RECORD_AUDIO and MODIFY_AUDIO_SETTINGS for recording your voice and the sound of video notes.
CAMERA for photos and video notes.
USE_BIOMETRIC and USE_FINGERPRINT for the system's unlock prompt. The app never sees your fingerprint or face.
WAKE_LOCK to finish a scheduled backup while the screen is off.
dev.engender.app.DYNAMIC_RECEIVER_NOT_EXPORTED_PERMISSION, which an Android library adds so that only the app can send its own internal messages.

sections.heading: Web app
paragraphs: The web app is served from app.engender.barankiewicz.dev, on an OVH server. Your journal stays in your browser and is never uploaded. Loading the app or an update is an ordinary web request, so the server sees your IP address, the time, the address requested and the User-Agent and Referer headers your browser sends. Access logs are turned off. Error logs can hold an IP address and the address requested, and are kept for at most seven days.
Fonts and the files for text recognition come from the same server. Scanning a lab result happens on your device.

sections.heading: Website and guide
paragraphs: The website, the guide and this policy at engender.barankiewicz.dev are hosted by lh.pl, which keeps access and error logs. Those can include IP addresses, requested addresses and browser headers. The site remembers your language and theme in your browser's local storage.

sections.heading: Page-opening counts
paragraphs: The website and the web app send one empty request each time they are opened online. The Android app sends none. The request carries no journal data, page name, referrer or cookie. The server that receives it sees your IP address and browser headers, as with any request, and drops them before adding one to a total for either "app" or "website" in a self-hosted GoatCounter.

Only those hourly totals are kept. They are kept indefinitely and only the developer can see them. There are no visitor identifiers, sessions, or breakdowns by location or device. A reload counts again, so the totals measure openings, not people.

sections.heading: Files you export
paragraphs: A backup or an export goes where you send it, and whatever app or service receives it handles it under its own terms. An encrypted backup (.ttbackup) can only be opened with the backup password you chose. Other exports are meant to be read, shared or printed, so they are not encrypted: CSV and JSON data, journal books, clinician summaries, photo collages and timelapses, PDFs and calendar files. Anyone who gets one of those can read it.

sections.heading: Deleting your data
paragraphs: In the app: Settings -> Privacy & data -> Delete everything.
On Android: uninstall the app, or clear its storage in the system settings.
On the web: clear the site data for app.engender.barankiewicz.dev in your browser.
None of these removes files you have already exported or backed up. Delete those where you saved them.

sections.heading: Support messages
paragraphs: If you write to engender-app@pm.me, the developer receives your email address, your message and any attachments, and uses them to answer you. Please don't send a real journal, backup, password or recovery key. If you send one by mistake, it is deleted when noticed. Support email is deleted within 30 days of the request being resolved, and you can ask for it to be deleted sooner.
GitHub issues are public, and GitHub's own policies apply to them.

sections.heading: Age
paragraphs: engender is for any trans person. There is no minimum or maximum age and no age verification.

sections.heading: Changes to this policy
paragraphs: When this policy changes, the date at the top changes with it. Earlier versions are in the history of https://github.com/engender-app/engender/blob/main/PRIVACY.md.
This policy is also available in Polish (https://github.com/engender-app/engender/blob/main/PRIVACY.pl.md).

getting-started.title: Getting started
getting-started.description: Installing engender, what onboarding asks, and why there's no account.

sections.heading: Installing
paragraphs: engender runs in a browser or as an Android app. In a browser there is nothing to download: open it and start writing. The Android app has to be installed first, and the home page lists where to get it.
You can also install the browser version from your browser's menu, or add it to your home screen. It then opens in its own window and works without a network connection.

Your journal lives where you start it. The Android app and your phone's browser hold two separate journals, and so do two browsers. To move a journal, export a backup, then choose "I already have a backup" the first time you open engender in the new place.

sections.heading: No account
paragraphs: There is no sign-up and no engender account. Nothing you write goes to a server. It is stored encrypted on your device and leaves only when you export it.
That also means nobody can hand your journal back if the device is lost or reset. Only a backup you exported survives, so export one every so often and keep it somewhere safe.

sections.heading: Setup
paragraphs: The first time you open engender, it asks a few questions before you reach your journal. A new journal has nine steps, and you can change every answer later.

paragraphs.rest: What the app is. If you have a backup, choose "I already have a backup" here instead of starting a new journal.
What the app should call you. It greets you with the name, and the name is saved in your backups.
Pick a flag. Its colours run through the whole app.
Which gender scales you want to rate when you write an entry.
Which parts of the app to show. The everyday ones are already on, and anything you leave off stays hidden until you turn it on in Settings.

How your journal opens: with a passphrase, a PIN, your device's own unlock, or without asking. Each option says what you gain and what you risk before you choose it. Nobody can recover a forgotten passphrase or PIN.
What the app may ask your phone for, such as notifications, each with a reason. You do not need any of it to write an entry.
Whether the app goes by Notes, with a different icon, outside itself: on your home screen and lock screen, for example. Inside the unlocked app nothing changes. It is off unless you turn it on.
Setup is over, and Go to Today opens your journal.

paragraphs: Most steps have Straight to the app, which ends setup early and keeps what you have chosen so far, and a Skip, which leaves that one setting as it was. Lock has neither, because the journal needs a way to open.
Setup is shorter when you restore a backup. The backup already holds your name, flag, scales and features, so once it is restored you are only asked about the lock, permissions and disguise.

images.alt: Welcome step calls engender your private transition journal and offers setup, a backup restore or going straight to the app.
Name step asks what the app should call you and says the answer can be skipped.

home.title: Today
home.description: The first tab: what is running, what is coming up, the mood pick, pinned rows and quick add.

sections.heading: What Today shows
paragraphs: Today is the first tab, and the app opens on it. It shows what is going on now and what is next. It greets you by name at the top, and the gear beside the greeting opens Settings.

paragraphs.rest: Things running right now, such as a wear timer or a dose that is due. A tile shows up when there is something to say and goes once it is dealt with.

Dated things in the next thirty days: appointments, surgery dates, milestones, letters due to open and doses on a schedule that is not daily. It shows three and folds the rest, and it is not there at all when nothing is coming.
Five moods, from awful to great. Picking one opens a new entry with that mood already chosen.
Short reminders you can dismiss, such as an old backup or a medication running low.
The parts of the app you keep on Today. Each row says what is next when there is something, and when you last logged it otherwise.

paragraphs: A new journal also has a Getting started section, with a few things worth setting up early. You can ignore them and just write.

images.alt: Today shows a binder timer, upcoming appointment and milestone, and the mood question.

sections.heading: Arranging Today
paragraphs: Tap Arrange these rows to choose what is pinned and in what order, and which live tiles can appear. A new journal starts with a few rows pinned. Once you have arranged them, the app never pins or moves anything by itself.

sections.heading: Quick add
paragraphs: The button in the middle of the bottom bar is quick add. It works from any screen and opens a fan of options: the five moods, an entry for an earlier day, the two tally counters, a dose while a regimen is running, and starting or stopping a wear session if you use wear time. Screens that log something keep their own add button as well.

sections.heading: Where an entry goes
paragraphs: An entry started from Today, from quick add or from Journal is the same kind of entry. Journal shows it on its day, and Look back counts it with the rest.

calendar.title: Journal
calendar.description: The month heat map, single days, search, starred entries and writing an entry.

sections.heading: The month
paragraphs: Journal is the second tab, and it holds your own days. The month sits at the top, folded into a strip. Show month opens it as a heat map: days with entries are filled in, coloured by your mood or, if you switch it, by one of your gender scales, and a deeper colour means a higher value. No colour means good or bad.
Under the month are your recent entries, and the button below them shows five more days at a time.

images.alt: Journal month view shows a mood heat map above recent entries.

sections.heading: One day
paragraphs: Tap a day to see everything logged on it. A day can hold as many entries as you like, and tapping an empty day in the past starts an entry for it. A day still ahead with a small mark has something planned, such as an appointment or a letter due to open, and tapping it shows what.

images.alt: Day view shows one journal entry and planned doses beneath it.

sections.heading: Search
paragraphs: The search icon at the top of Journal opens search. Before you type, it offers your most-used tags and recent searches. Filters narrow the results by tag, mood, mode, body region, a range on one of your scales, dates, starred, or whether an entry has a note or a photo.
Search also looks outside your entries, at document titles for example, and lists what it finds under Elsewhere in the journal.
Star an entry you want to find again, then filter by Starred to see all of them.

sections.heading: Writing an entry
paragraphs: An entry is one moment. It needs a mood, and everything else is optional.
A new entry opens on How is today?, with the five moods and your gender scales. Save entry stops there, and that is a complete entry. Add a note, tags, photos goes on to the full page.

On the full page the note comes first, under the date, then mode and the gender scales. The moods and the star sit on the save bar at the bottom. A row of chips opens the rest one at a time: tags, the body map, photos, voice and video. Editing a saved entry opens this page straight away.
The body map is where you mark how a part of your body feels. Pick a spot, then slide towards dysphoria or towards euphoria. Leaving it in the middle records nothing.

stats.title: Look back
stats.description: Choosing a stretch of time, the readings, the tally, Wrapped and On this day.

sections.heading: Choosing a stretch
paragraphs: Look back is the third tab. Everything on it reads one stretch of time, which you choose on the timeline at the top: drag its two ends, or pick a stretch from the list. The timeline also shows your eras, milestones, regimen, tryouts and surgeries, and tapping one picks its dates.
Just under the timeline are the plain facts for that stretch: how many entries, the average on a scale, which scale moved the furthest, and how many days fell at each mood.

images.alt: Look back shows a selected date range, entry count and reading summary.

sections.heading: Readings
paragraphs: Below that is a grid of readings. Each tile shows one figure for the stretch, and tapping it opens the full reading. A tile with nothing to show for the stretch is left out.

paragraphs.rest: One scale or your mood across the stretch, day after day. You can add a second scale to it.
Each day as a point on two scales, which you can play through in order.
The tags you used most in the stretch, on every day or only on good days.

paragraphs.lead: Tags, and how a scale moved.
paragraphs.rest: Which tags came with a scale going up or down.
How each part of the body has felt over the stretch, towards dysphoria or towards euphoria.
Two periods side by side. It starts with your stretch against the same length of time just before it.
How often you were misgendered and how often people got it right, over time. Quick add adds to either count from any screen.
What you recorded spending in the stretch, by area and by whether it was refunded. Each currency keeps its own total.

sections.heading: Wrapped and On this day
paragraphs: Two more tiles sit under the grid. You can turn either one off in Settings.

paragraphs.rest: A look back at a finished week, month or year: entries, mood, the scale that moved furthest, tags, milestones, photos and letters.
A good day from a month, six months, a year or more years ago, or a day with a letter written or opened on it. A day that went badly and has no letter is not brought back.

health.title: Health and body
health.description: Your medication, cycle, surgery and appointments, then the Body group: progress photos, changes you've noticed, hair removal, wear log and voice.

sections.heading: The Transition tab
paragraphs: The fourth tab, Transition, has five groups: Health, Body, Steps, Support and Media. Search at the top finds a row by name and searches the text of your journal.
This chapter covers the first two groups, Health and Body.

sections.heading: Meds
paragraphs: Meds is where your medication lives. Each drug in a running regimen gets its own lane. The timeline marks your latest lab draw. For each regimen, Meds shows the dose and route, your last dose, when the next one is expected, how much you have left with the projected run-out day, and how much of the drug you took in the last 90 days.

paragraphs.rest: What you take, how and how often, from the day you started. Tap a lane to change it. You can pause a regimen or end it, and it stays in your history. If you switch it on, a schedule records an expected dose as taken after that day ends. You can correct it or mark it skipped.
Every dose taken, skipped or changed, at the time it happened. You can read it as logged or against the schedule.

Your results, as you entered them. Import from photo reads a lab slip from your camera or gallery. The photo is read on your device, and the result keeps the slip's own value and unit. Results in different units stay on separate lines.
A count you enter now and then. Logged doses feed the estimate of what is left and the projected run-out day, and the app tells you when stock is running low.

images.alt: Meds shows medication lanes with lab draw, last dose, next dose and stock dates.

sections.heading: Cycle
paragraphs: Cycle logs a period, spotting, or nothing this month. The row only shows while a testosterone regimen is running, or once you turn on Cycle tracking in Settings.

sections.heading: Surgery journey
paragraphs: Each surgery gets its own journey, named however you like. It holds the consults before it, the date once you have one, and afterwards a day count, photos, notes and your own checklist.
Dilation becomes a row of its own once a surgery calls for it. Type in the schedule your surgeon gave you and log your sessions against it.

sections.heading: Appointments
paragraphs: Appointments opens on your next visit and how far away it is. Under it is What to raise, your list of things to bring up, which carries over from one visit to the next.

At the visit, In the room goes through your questions one at a time, with space for what they said. Past visits are under Behind you, and the app asks how each one went. An appointment can also wait without a date: Waiting lists keeps referrals, the day you were referred, dated updates and how long you have waited, and never guesses when you will be seen. Who you see holds your own notes on the people you go to, and an appointment can name one of them.

The clinician visit summary is a page to print for a doctor, for dates you choose. It can include your regimen, cumulative exposure, lab results, side effects, the changes you noticed and procedures, and you pick which sections go in. You see it exactly as it will print. Open it from Meds or from Appointments.

sections.heading: Progress photos
paragraphs: Body is the second group, and Progress photos is its first row. It keeps photos taken in the same pose. Pick two and drag the divider across them to compare an earlier one with a later one.

sections.heading: Changes you've noticed
paragraphs: Pick a change from the list or add your own, and mark the day you first noticed it. Side effects go here too, each with how strong it was, from 1 to 5, and whether it is ongoing or resolved. The more private categories, such as genital and sexual changes, start switched off.
What the literature says shows when a change is usually reported, taken from SOC8 or the studies it cites.

paragraphs.rest: What your hair is doing, in your own words, with photos taken from the same angle.

images.alt: Changes you have noticed shows a dated timeline of effects recorded in the journal.

sections.heading: Hair removal
paragraphs: Hair removal logs electrolysis and laser sessions, with the area, method, how long it took, pain if you want to note it, cost, provider and photos. The screen shows how long it has been since the last one.

sections.heading: Wear log
paragraphs: Wear log is for binder, tucking and compression wear. Start a timer, or fill in a session afterwards, with a note on comfort or pain. You can set a reminder for a number of hours you choose. With a binder, a quiet cue appears at eight hours, and you can turn it off. The screen also shows the hours worn each week.
Binder safety guidance and its sources are on the same screen.

sections.heading: Voice
paragraphs: Voice has four tabs: Benchmark, Practise, Compare and Recordings.

A benchmark is a take made the same way every time: you read the same passage and hold the same three vowels. That keeps takes months apart comparable. It shows figures such as pitch and speaking rate, and Compare puts two benchmarks side by side. It gives no verdict on your voice.

sections.heading: What Health and Body do not do
paragraphs: Nothing in these two groups says whether a number is good or bad, suggests a dose or tells you what to do. They keep what you enter and draw it.

steps.title: Steps
steps.description: The transition roadmap, milestones and eras, and tryouts.

sections.heading: The roadmap
paragraphs: Steps is the third group on the Transition tab. It holds the transition roadmap, milestones and tryouts.

The roadmap comes with two groups of steps, each behind its own switch. Social and presentation has eight steps, such as telling family, your name and pronouns, clothes and voice. Polish legal steps holds the Polish legal procedure for changing the sex marker, and is on by default when the app is in Polish.

After the ruling, Name and document changes lists the institutions to update, such as PESEL, your ID card, passport, bank and employer, and you can add your own. Each one records when you submitted the change, how long you have been waiting and when it was done, with the documents filed under it.

Steps can be done in any order. Tick a step once it is done, or mark it not my path. You can hide a step you do not need and bring it back later. With Offer a milestone switched on, ticking a step asks whether to add it to your milestones.
You can add categories of your own with steps in them, whether the built-in groups are on or not, and file documents against a step.
The roadmap describes the procedure and never says what to do in your own case. It shows the date its content was last checked against its sources.

images.alt: Transition roadmap shows the Polish legal steps switch and a Coming out list with one step ticked.

sections.heading: Milestones and eras
paragraphs: A milestone is a day that mattered, or will. One still ahead counts down, and one behind you comes back each year as an anniversary. You can choose whether it is celebrated when the day comes.
Eras are stretches of time you name yourself, such as "before I knew". They show as bands behind your milestones, and Look back can use one as its stretch. You make and edit them in Settings.

sections.heading: Tryouts
paragraphs: A tryout is something you are trying: a name, pronouns, a style or makeup. It has a start date and, once you stop, an end date. Note how it feels as often as you like, on the tryout itself or in an entry, and add photos. Several can run at once. If one sticks, you can adopt it: the tryout ends, and a name you adopt can become the name the app calls you.

support.title: Support
support.description: Time-capsule letters, Safe space for the hard days, and the directory of helplines and support organisations.

sections.heading: Time-capsule letters
paragraphs: Support is the fourth group on the Transition tab. It holds Time-capsule letters, Safe space, and Support and resources.
Write a letter to yourself and pick the day it opens. It stays sealed until then, and after that you can read it whenever you like. Letters about to open show on Today, under Coming up.

sections.heading: Safe space
paragraphs: Safe space is for the moments when dysphoria is too much. At the top is Things that help, your own list: who to text, which walk, which song. It starts empty. Under it is box breathing.
Below the breathing are two rows. Support and resources opens the directory described below. Good moments shows past entries you tagged as good, or starred, and appears once you have one.
Opening Safe space writes nothing to your journal.

images.alt: Good moments in Safe space lists starred and tagged journal entries.

sections.heading: Support and resources
paragraphs: Support and resources lists helplines and support organisations in two groups: Poland, and UK and US. Each has a line on what it offers and a number or an address, and there is some reading as well. It comes with the app, so you can read it with no signal. Some of the helplines are general ones, open to anyone. Emergency numbers such as 112 are not on the list.
The screen says when the entries were last checked. Tapping a number or an address hands it to your phone or browser, which leaves the app.

images.alt: Support and resources lists contacts, with tabs for Poland and for the UK and US.

media.title: Media
media.description: Every photo in your journal in one list, and the documents you keep.

sections.heading: Photos
paragraphs: Media is the fifth group on the Transition tab.

Photos is every photo in your journal in one dated list: from entries, milestones, hair progress, hair removal, tryouts, surgery, progress photos and video notes. Once the photos come from more than one place, chips at the top narrow the list by where a photo came from, and Starred shows the ones you have starred.
Select photos to delete them. A deleted photo goes from everywhere it appears, and you can undo that for 10 seconds. Open record takes you to the entry or record a photo belongs to.

Make a collage or timelapse, at the bottom of the list, builds one from the photos in a date range. Tap a photo to leave it out, and preview the result before you save or share it. The file you save is not encrypted. To compare two photos, use Progress photos in the Body group.
Photos stay inside the app and never go to your phone's gallery.

images.alt: Progress photos shows source filters and a grid of dated photos.

sections.heading: Documents
paragraphs: Documents holds the papers you keep, such as opinions, diagnoses, referrals, court rulings and invoices. Each has a date, a title you write and the file itself: a PDF or an image, up to 25 MB. You can link a document to a roadmap step, a milestone, a surgery journey or a regimen.

The list groups documents by what they are linked to, with unlinked ones last. Photos and PDFs have thumbnails. Share or save makes a copy that is not encrypted. The app never reads what a document says, so you find one by its title.

settings.title: Settings
settings.description: The five sections of Settings, and what lives elsewhere instead.

sections.heading: What belongs here
paragraphs: Settings holds preferences and the lists those preferences draw from: how the journal looks, what it asks you to track and when it reminds you. What you record stays on its own screen. Doses, lab results and surgery notes are on the Transition tab, not here.
The gear at the top of Today opens Settings. It has five sections.

images.alt: Settings shows flag palettes, mood colours and theme controls under Appearance.

sections.heading: Appearance
paragraphs: Appearance holds the app's language, theme, gender palette and mood colours. There are sixteen palettes, and mood colours have their own presets. You can also make text larger, make text and borders clearer, and reduce motion. On Android you can change the app icon here too.

sections.heading: Tracking
paragraphs: Tracking holds Gender scales, Tag groups and Features to show. Features to show is where you choose which parts of the app appear, and it has the switch for cycle tracking.

sections.heading: Reminders & prompts
paragraphs: Reminders is where you set when the app should nudge you. Notices and notifications switches the app's other prompts on or off and sets quiet hours, a stretch when no notification arrives. A reminder due in quiet hours waits until they end. Phone notifications need the Android app.
Live tiles are not here. You switch them in Today's editor, beside its pins.

sections.heading: Your lists
paragraphs: Your lists holds the lists used across the journal: modes, entry templates, body regions and eras.

sections.heading: Privacy & data
paragraphs: Lock & recovery holds how your journal opens, when it locks and the recovery key. Permissions and Disguise app are in this section too.

Export / import is where you make or restore a backup, export plain CSV or JSON and import from Daylio. On Android it is also where you choose a backup folder, and newer backups that your other devices save there can be merged in.
Journal book prints a range you choose. Trash keeps deleted entries for 30 days, and you can delete one for good sooner. Delete everything erases the journal from this device.
Below the sections, About shows the app's version and links to this guide, the privacy policy and the source code.

privacy.title: Privacy
privacy.description: Where the journal lives, how it is encrypted and opened, what other people can see, and what happens to files you export.

sections.heading: Where the journal lives
paragraphs: Your journal stays in storage on the device where you use it. There is no account and no profile on a server, and nothing you write is uploaded. The Android app and a browser keep separate journals, and so do two browser profiles.

The web app still has to come from a server. When it loads or updates, its host can see your IP address, the time of the request, which files the browser asks for and their sizes, plus the User-Agent and referrer headers. Entries, photos, notes and lab results are never part of that. The website and the web app also count how often they are opened, as totals with no record of individual visits. The privacy policy has the details.

sections.heading: Encryption and access
paragraphs: The database is encrypted whole, including its side files and the copy made before an upgrade changes it. Photos and thumbnails sit outside the database, so each file is encrypted separately with the same random data key.

A few things are not encrypted, and none of them is journal content: the wrapped key and the settings needed to open it, your theme, palette and language, lock timing, the disguise choice, and the times of wrong PIN attempts. On Android, a photo you take also passes through an unencrypted temporary file before the app imports and encrypts it.

How your journal opens is your choice, under Lock & recovery in Settings. On the web it can be a passphrase, a four-digit PIN together with a key kept in the browser profile, your device unlock through WebAuthn PRF on a browser that supports it, or unlocked, with a key in the browser profile and no prompt. On Android it can be your screen lock or biometrics through Android Keystore, a four-digit PIN with a Keystore key, a passphrase, or unlocked, with a Keystore key and no prompt.

A passphrase goes through Argon2id and wraps the data key with AES-GCM, so you can change it without encrypting the journal again. The other modes depend on a key held in the browser profile or in Android Keystore. Clearing the site's data, resetting the profile, clearing the app's data or losing the device makes that copy of the journal unreadable.
The same screen sets when your journal locks: immediately, after 1 minute, after 5 minutes, or only when the app restarts.

A recovery key is optional. It has 25 characters and is shown once, when you make it. If your passphrase, PIN or biometrics stop working, it opens the journal on the device, and on the web the browser profile, that still holds it. It cannot move the journal or open an Archive. Without a recovery key, nobody can recover lost credentials, and nobody can recover a forgotten Archive password either. After you copy the key, the app clears it from the clipboard a minute later where the system lets it.

sections.heading: What other people can see
paragraphs: Disguise app changes what someone near your phone sees. The launcher icon and name become Notes, and the lock screen, widgets, notifications and, on the web, the tab's icon and title stop naming engender. On Android it also blocks screenshots and the preview in Recents. Inside the unlocked app nothing changes. Disguise is not encryption, and Android still shows the real name in App info and in permission prompts.
Notifications hide sensitive titles unless you switch Hide sensitive titles off. Reminder times and the daily check-in question still show on a locked screen.

images.alt: Settings' Disguise app sheet shows the disguise switch and the neutral Notes name on the browser tab and lock screen.

sections.heading: Android and network access
paragraphs: The Android app does not request the INTERNET permission. It opens no network sockets and sends no journal data to a server. It also opts out of Android's cloud backup and device-to-device transfer. A store you install it from can still record installs and updates under its own policies.

Android asks for POST_NOTIFICATIONS, SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM and RECEIVE_BOOT_COMPLETED so reminders and the daily check-in arrive at the time you chose and come back after a restart. WAKE_LOCK lets a scheduled backup finish with the screen off. RECORD_AUDIO and MODIFY_AUDIO_SETTINGS are for voice notes, and CAMERA is for video notes and for photos, which open the phone's camera app. USE_BIOMETRIC and USE_FINGERPRINT let it show the phone's own fingerprint, face or screen lock prompt.

sections.heading: Archives and other exports
paragraphs: You choose where an exported or shared file goes. A cloud drive or document provider can see its filename, timestamp and size, along with account access records.

An encrypted .ttbackup Archive uses chunked AES-256-GCM and a password you choose. The password protects that Archive, not the journal on your device. Its header stays readable: the first six bytes say GDIARY, followed by the format version, Argon2id settings and salt. The app needs those to recognise the file and derive its key. The header reveals the format, not your entries, and nobody without the password can read the rest.

On Android, Auto-export writes an Archive to a folder you pick, every week or every month. With Merge backups from other devices switched on, the app looks in that folder when you open it and merges in a newer Archive that another device saved there with the same password. Nothing is sent anywhere. Both devices only read and write the folder.

Some exports are deliberately readable: CSV and JSON data, journal books for printing or PDF, clinician summaries, photo collages and timelapses, saved PDFs, and single-event .ics calendar files. Anyone who receives one can read what it contains. The app asks you to confirm or take an explicit action before it makes an unencrypted file.

images.alt: Export and import shows backup age and the encrypted export form.

sections.heading: Deleting everything
paragraphs: Delete everything, under Privacy & data in Settings, erases the journal, its photos and recordings, your settings and the keys from this device. It cannot be undone, and the app offers to back up first. Uninstalling the Android app, or clearing the site's data in a browser, removes the same things. Files you already exported stay wherever you saved them.

sections.heading: Security reports
paragraphs: You can report a security problem through GitHub's private vulnerability reporting. Include the app version, device or browser, clear steps to reproduce the problem, and what you expected and saw. Use invented data for a minimal proof.
One person maintains the project, so a report is read when they next sit down to work. There is no fixed response window.

contributing.title: Contributing
contributing.description: Reporting a problem, code, country packs and translations.

sections.heading: Reporting a problem
paragraphs: Report a bug in the issues at github.com/engender-app/engender. Say which version you have (Settings, then About), whether you are on Android or in a browser, and the steps that lead to the problem. Issues are public, so describe the problem with invented data and never paste anything from your journal.

sections.heading: Code
paragraphs: engender is free software under GPLv3. Clone the Journal repository from github.com/engender-app/engender. With Node.js 24, run npm ci, then npm run dev to work locally. The README lists the checks: npm run check, npm test and npm run test:browser cover different parts of the app, and the first two need one build on a fresh checkout.

Keep a pull request to one change, on a branch that is up to date with main. CI runs on each pull request, including browser checks, and has to pass before a merge. Use invented journal data in tests and screenshots.

sections.heading: Country packs
paragraphs: You don't need to write code to help with a country pack. A pack is bundled into the app and describes one country's transition procedure as roadmap steps. Only the Polish pack ships today. It covers the legal procedure and the institutions to update after it.

Cite sources for each step you propose and record when you checked them. The roadmap shows the date its content was last checked, because procedures change. Describe what a step involves, never what someone should do in their own case. You can send sourced corrections or draft steps without editing the app.

sections.heading: Translations
paragraphs: The Journal keeps screen text in messages/en.json and messages/pl.json, and npm run strings opens an editor for both. The app supports English and Polish today. Another language needs its own catalogue, some changes in the code that lists the languages, and a check of each screen with the real text, including long labels on small phones.
Translate the meaning, then edit until it reads naturally in the new language.

holds.heading: Journal
holds.body: How today felt. A mood, a note, your own scales, tags, photos, a voice memo, and where in your body dysphoria or euphoria sat. The mood is the only part you need.

holds.heading: Look back
holds.body: Whether anything is changing is hard to see day to day. Looking at a few months on one chart, everything is much more obvious. Look back is just for that - it lets you take an analytical look at your gender in order to understand it better. Charts allow you to notice correlations such as how your dysphoria levels change depending on various factors.

holds.heading: HRT
holds.body: Your medication schedule with the next dose and how much is left, doses logged as you take them, reminders you can answer with Taken or Skip, and lab results drawn as a chart. The app never suggests a dose or shows a reference range.

holds.heading: Surgeries
holds.body: A journal per procedure: consults, the date itself, recovery, and photos that stay inside the app rather than in your camera roll.

holds.heading: Tryouts
holds.body: Try a name, a pronoun set, a style or a garment. Give it a start date, log how it feels as you go, and close it when you know to either reject it or accept it for good.

holds.heading: Eras
holds.body: Name the chapters of your own timeline. They are marked along your timeline and milestones, so a reading sits against the era you were in when you wrote it.

holds.heading: Voice
holds.body: Practice, record the same passage each time, and compare with your own earlier takes. Pitch, resonance and speaking rate describe the recording without grading your voice.

holds.heading: Clinician summary
holds.body: Bring your doses, labs, side effects and changes to an appointment as one printed summary, over a range you choose, with only the sections you choose.

holdsAlso: Also in there: search across your notes and tags, a tally of the times you were misgendered and gendered right, milestones with countdowns ahead and anniversaries behind, letters that open on a date you choose, a roadmap of the legal steps in Poland with room for your own, the offices to update after a name change, binder and tucking wear time, hair removal sessions, waiting lists, notes on the people you see, what each visit or prescription cost, appointment prep, Safe Space with your good days and your own comfort list, a directory of trans organisations and helplines you can read offline, one photo library across all of it, and a place for referrals and court orders. If you already have a diary in Daylio, it imports.
